paras: The lynching of Lewis Jackson was the hanging of a Black man by white men near Tampa, Florida, on the night of December 4, 1903, shortly after the sheriff released him from jail. Jackson had been accused of an assault on the three- or four-year-old daughter of R. F. Ensey of the government works at the entrance to Tampa Bay, and the papers said he was freed because no state law covered the offense. The wire report said a mob of fifty white men hanged him, while special telegrams to New York papers described two or three successive mobs, one of which mutilated him before another hanged him.

Jackson, described as twenty-five years old, was accused of an assault or attempted assault on Ensey's young daughter on the Monday before the lynching. The papers placed the incident at Fort Dade, at Fort De Soto on Mullet Key, or on Egmont Key, and gave the girl's age as three or four.

Soldiers captured him; the Baltimore Afro-American, in a brief printed before the lynching, said soldiers in a boat "lassoed" him after he jumped into the bay to escape a posse. According to the New York Sun, artillerymen at the fort gave him "a severe beating" before he was brought to the Tampa jail; the Ocala Evening Star said he was "almost beaten to death."

No statute was found under which he could be convicted, owing, the wire said, to "the peculiarity of the crime." The sheriff released him on the night of December 4, and the wire report said he was warned that his life was in danger.

In the New-York Tribune's account, a waiting mob captured him near the jail and emasculated him, the same punishment it said had been inflicted on a Black hackman six months earlier. He was then put in a carriage bound for the "colored hospital," where physicians were waiting, but a second mob stopped the carriage and hanged him to an oak tree. The Sun's version was similar but set the mutilation in a thicket near the city limits and named the earlier victim as George Houston.

In the wire version, two white men caught him at the edge of town and took him by cab to a spot near the city, where a mob hanged him to a tree. The Ocala paper said his body was found hanging in the suburbs two hours after he left the jail.
A coroner's jury returned what the Tribune called "the usual verdict" of death at the hands of persons unknown. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story spread on December 5 and 6 as a short Tampa wire dispatch, printed by the Savannah Morning News, the Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Indianapolis Journal and other papers. Southern headlines stressed the charge: the Americus Times-Recorder said Jackson "Pays Death Penalty," the Savannah paper called him "a Mob's Victim Because of His Brutal Attempt," and Montgomery's headline read "Mob Killed Negro Whom Law Could Not Reach." The New York papers headlined the sequence of mobs ("Two Mobs Wait for Negro," "Three Mobs Got Him"), and the Ocala Evening Star stated that he had "attempted a nameless outrage."

The Black press carried the case only in brief: on December 12 the St. Paul Appeal reprinted the wire under its own headline, "Lynch Man Law Can't Touch," and the Richmond Planet listed it in its weekly news chronology. The Chicago Broad Ax included "Lewis Jackson (colored), near Tampa" in its year-end chronology of 1903, dated December 5, with the charge "attempted assault." No Black-press editorial or correspondent's account of the lynching was found.

Accounts differ on how many mobs acted and whether Jackson was mutilated: the wire report mentioned only a mob of fifty that hanged him, the Tribune two mobs, and the Sun three, counting the soldiers. The Alexandria Gazette placed the "surgical operation" before the night of the lynching, saying another mob caught him "last night." A special telegram to the Lewiston Evening Teller said he was "taken from the jail" and mutilated, while the fuller reports say he had already been released.

reader.title: Lynching of Lewis Jackson
bases: Every account says a mob of white men hanged Jackson near Tampa after he was released from jail on an accusation of assaulting a child (A7, A8, A9).

Jackson was hanged from a tree by a mob, given as fifty white men in the wire report, with no legal authority (A9, A7); the mob acted on the accusation of assault after the law was said to offer no means of conviction (A7, A8).

The wire report (A9), separate special telegrams to the New-York Tribune and the Sun (A7, A8), and a Florida paper (A3) agree that Jackson was released from the Tampa jail and hanged by a mob; they differ on details of the mobs and mutilation.

accounts.label: Wire report (Tampa, Dec. 5)
accounts.gist: Released for want of a law and warned his life was in danger, Jackson was seized by two white men at the outskirts of town, carried in a cab to a spot near the city and hanged to a tree by a mob of fifty white men; no mutilation is mentioned.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune special telegram
accounts.gist: A waiting mob captured him near the jail and emasculated him, then sent him by carriage toward the colored hospital; a second mob intercepted the carriage and hanged him to an oak.

accounts.label: The Sun special dispatch
accounts.gist: Three mobs: artillerymen who beat him at the fort, a mob that injured him in a thicket near the city limits, and a third that took him from the cab and hanged him from an oak limb.

accounts.label: Ocala Evening Star (Florida)
accounts.gist: Soldiers captured him on Egmont Key and almost beat him to death; released from the Tampa jail, he was found hanging from a tree in the suburbs two hours later.

accounts.label: Lewiston Evening Teller special telegram
accounts.gist: Jackson was taken from the jail, mutilated and lynched; his body was found in a secluded spot.

accounts.label: Baltimore Afro-American brief (before the lynching)
accounts.gist: Soldiers in a boat lassoed Jackson after he jumped into the bay to escape a posse.

framing.detail: Americus Times-Recorder deck: 'Lewis Jackson, Who Attempted a Criminal Assault ... Pays Death Penalty', treating the charge as fact.
Savannah Morning News: 'Negro a Mob's Victim Because of His Brutal Attempt.'
Montgomery Advertiser, Birmingham Age-Herald and Indianapolis Journal ran the wire under headlines such as 'Mob Killed Negro Whom Law Could Not Reach.'
New-York Tribune and Sun headlined the sequence of mobs ('Two Mobs Wait for Negro', 'Three Mobs Got Him') and stated the assault as fact; the Tribune called the inquest finding 'the usual verdict'.
Ocala Evening Star, the one Florida paper found, gave a short item stating that he 'attempted a nameless outrage'.
St. Paul Appeal reprinted the wire under 'Lynch Man Law Can't Touch'.
Richmond Planet and Chicago Broad Ax listed the lynching in news and year-end chronologies; the Afro-American reported only the capture.
